meta.title: 3D to 2D Dish - Projection Catalog
meta.reference: Classification per Snyder (1987) Map Projections: A Working Manual (USGS), and standard GIS cartography texts.
meta.note: epsg fields are left null where a projection is parameterized per study area rather than having one universal code (e.g. Albers, Lambert Conformal Conic). Fill those in per deployment.

propertyClasses.name: Equidistant
propertyClasses.preserves: true distance from one point or along specific lines

propertyClasses.name: True-Direction (Azimuthal)
propertyClasses.preserves: true bearing from one center point
propertyClasses.distorts: distance and shape away from center

families.name: Cylindrical
families.surface: Cylinder tangent or secant to a great circle (usually the equator; a meridian in transverse aspect)

projections.name: Mercator
projections.author: Gerardus Mercator
projections.epsg: EPSG:3857 (spherical Web Mercator variant used by web map tiles)
projections.distortionNote: Area exaggerates severely poleward (Greenland reads far larger than its true ~14x-smaller size vs Africa); local angles stay true, which is why rhumb lines are straight.

projections.name: Transverse Mercator
projections.distortionNote: Same conformal math as Mercator, rotated so the tangent line runs along a meridian instead of the equator.

projections.name: Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM)
projections.distortionNote: Conformal, not equal-area. Earth split into 60 six-degree-wide zones; each zone is a secant transverse Mercator, keeping scale distortion under about 0.1% within the zone.

projections.name: Lambert Cylindrical Equal-Area
projections.author: Johann Heinrich Lambert
projections.distortionNote: True area everywhere, but shapes stretch severely near the poles. The Gall-Peters projection is a secant variant (standard parallels ~45deg), popularized in the 1970s 'fair map' debate.

projections.name: Plate Carree (Equirectangular)
projections.epsg: EPSG:4326 used loosely as this grid
projections.distortionNote: x = longitude, y = latitude, directly. Only true to scale along the equator (or chosen standard parallel); everything else stretches.

projections.name: Miller Cylindrical
bestFor: general reference maps wanting a Mercator look with less polar exaggeration
projections.distortionNote: A modified Mercator; reduces but does not eliminate polar area exaggeration, and is not truly conformal.

families.name: Conic
families.surface: Cone over the globe, tangent (one standard parallel) or secant (two), apex over a pole

projections.name: Lambert Conformal Conic
projections.distortionNote: True local shape/angle between the two standard parallels; widely used as the basis for many national grid systems.

projections.name: Albers Equal-Area Conic
projections.distortionNote: The standard US Census Bureau choice for country-wide choropleth maps; true area, shape drifts away from the standard parallels.

projections.name: Equidistant Conic
bestFor: regional maps where along-meridian distance accuracy matters
projections.distortionNote: True distance along meridians and along the standard parallels.

projections.name: American Polyconic
bestFor: historical interest: early USGS topographic quadrangles
projections.distortionNote: Each parallel is its own true-to-scale cone rather than a single consistent conic surface; low distortion near the central meridian, not strictly conformal or equal-area.

families.name: Azimuthal (Planar)
families.surface: Flat plane touching the globe at a single point (or secant to a small circle around it)

projections.name: Azimuthal Equidistant
projections.distortionNote: True distance AND true direction from the single center point only; both degrade with distance from center.

projections.name: Lambert Azimuthal Equal-Area
projections.distortionNote: True area from the center outward; shape distorts increasingly toward the map's edge.

projections.name: Stereographic
projections.distortionNote: True local shape/angle everywhere; area exaggerates away from the center point.

projections.name: Orthographic
bestFor: a natural 'photo from space' globe view - good default starting view for a globe-to-flat animation
projections.distortionNote: Perspective from infinite distance; only the center point is distortion-free, everything toward the limb compresses.

projections.name: Gnomonic
bestFor: great-circle route planning for aviation and shipping
projections.distortionNote: Perspective from the Earth's center; every great circle, including all meridians, renders as a straight line. Cannot show a full hemisphere.

projections.name: General Perspective (near-side)
bestFor: satellite-view style renderings with an adjustable viewing altitude
projections.distortionNote: Perspective from a finite height above the surface; a good UI slider parameter (altitude) for the 3D globe view.

families.name: Pseudocylindrical
families.surface: Parallels are straight horizontal lines like cylindrical, but meridians curve toward the poles

projections.name: Sinusoidal (Sanson-Flamsteed)
bestFor: one of the oldest equal-area world map projections
projections.distortionNote: Parallels equally spaced and straight; meridians are sine curves. Shape distorts increasingly away from the central meridian and equator.

projections.name: Mollweide
bestFor: global raster and astronomical all-sky data visualization
projections.distortionNote: Elliptical world outline; true area everywhere, shape compresses near the outline's edges.

projections.name: Eckert IV
bestFor: thematic atlases wanting a rounded, visually balanced equal-area map
projections.distortionNote: True area with rounded meridians for a softer visual than Sinusoidal or Mollweide.

projections.name: Robinson
bestFor: general-reference world maps prioritizing pleasing appearance
projections.distortionNote: Not truly equal-area or conformal; was National Geographic's standard world map from 1988 to 1998, chosen for overall visual balance rather than any single true property.

projections.name: Goode Homolosine
projections.distortionNote: Splices Sinusoidal (low latitudes) and Mollweide (high latitudes), usually interrupted into ocean-centered or land-centered 'orange peel' lobes.

families.name: Compromise
families.surface: Not derived from a single literal developable surface; mathematically balances several distortions at once

projections.name: Winkel Tripel
projections.author: Oswald Winkel
bestFor: National Geographic's standard world map since 1998
projections.distortionNote: Minimizes combined area, angle, and distance distortion simultaneously rather than perfecting any one of them.

projections.name: Van der Grinten
bestFor: historical interest: NGS's standard world map from 1922 to 1988
projections.distortionNote: Circular world outline; area distortion at high latitudes is nearly as severe as Mercator, despite the different look.

projections.name: Natural Earth (Patterson)
projections.author: Tom Patterson
bestFor: default general-reference world map in many modern open-source GIS tools
projections.distortionNote: Purpose-built in the 2000s specifically to look good as a general-purpose reference map, not to satisfy any single classical property.

stretchGoals.name: Retroazimuthal family
stretchGoals.note: Preserves true direction TO a fixed point rather than from it (e.g. Craig Retroazimuthal / Qibla-finder maps). Niche; flagged as a Phase 2+ catalog extension.

stretchGoals.name: Polyhedral / interrupted family
stretchGoals.note: Dymaxion (Fuller), AuthaGraph, and similar. Visually striking but complex to render; flagged as a Phase 2+ catalog extension.
